title: Company and Commercial Law
topics: Separate legal personality and the veil
Sale of goods and passing of property

notes.h: Separate legal personality and piercing the veil
notes.body:
A registered company is a legal person distinct from its members and directors (Companies Act 2006, s.16; Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22). It owns property, contracts, sues and is sued in its own right. Where liability is limited by shares, members risk only any unpaid amount on their shares.

Consequences of separate personality:
- Lee v Lee's Air Farming Ltd [1961] AC 12: a controlling shareholder-director can also be the company's employee.
- Macaura v Northern Assurance Co [1925] AC 619: a shareholder has no insurable interest in company assets.
- Groups: each subsidiary is a separate entity and there is no general "single economic unit" doctrine (Adams v Cape Industries plc [1990] Ch 433, preferring Woolfson v Strathclyde RC 1978 to DHN Food Distributors v Tower Hamlets LBC [1976]).

Piercing the veil. In Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd [2013] UKSC 34 Lord Sumption confined true piercing to the evasion principle: a person under an existing legal obligation or restriction deliberately evades it, or frustrates its enforcement, by interposing a company under their control. The court may disregard the company only to remove that advantage, and only as a last resort. Gilford Motor Co v Horne [1933] Ch 935 and Jones v Lipman [1962] 1 WLR 832 fit this principle. "Concealment" cases merely look behind the company to identify the real actors and do not pierce at all. In Prest itself the wife obtained the properties because the companies held them on resulting trust for the husband.

Other routes to a similar result:
- Statute: fraudulent and wrongful trading (Insolvency Act 1986 ss 213–214) and the phoenix-name rule (s.216).
- Agency or trust proved on the facts (Smith, Stone & Knight v Birmingham Corp [1939] 4 All ER 116; rarely succeeds).
- Tort: a parent may owe its own duty of care to people affected by a subsidiary's operations where it assumed responsibility, for example by controlling or issuing group-wide policies (Chandler v Cape plc [2012] EWCA Civ 525; Vedanta Resources plc v Lungowe [2019] UKSC 20; Okpabi v Royal Dutch Shell plc [2021] UKSC 3).

Illustration. Ravi sells his café business with a two-year non-compete, then opens a rival café through a company his partner owns on his behalf. He is evading an existing obligation, so the court can restrain both Ravi and the company (Gilford).

Exam pitfalls:
- Parent-company negligence cases are not veil piercing; they impose direct liability.
- Piercing cannot make the controller a party to the company's contracts (VTB Capital plc v Nutritek International Corp [2013] UKSC 5).
- Structuring a group to limit future liabilities is legitimate (Adams v Cape).

notes.h: The company constitution and corporate capacity
notes.body:
Under CA 2006 s.17 the constitution comprises the articles of association plus the resolutions and agreements listed in s.29 (such as special resolutions). For pre-2009 companies, old memorandum provisions such as objects clauses are treated as part of the articles (s.28).

Articles
- Model articles apply by default to the extent not excluded (s.20; Companies (Model Articles) Regulations 2008).
- Articles are altered by special resolution, a 75% majority of votes (ss 21, 283).
- An alteration must be made bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole (Allen v Gold Reefs of West Africa [1900] 1 Ch 656). The shareholders' honest view is respected unless no reasonable shareholder could hold it (Citco Banking Corp v Pusser's Ltd [2007] UKPC 13).

The s.33 contract
- The constitution binds the company and its members as if each had covenanted to observe it; members can enforce it against each other (Rayfield v Hands [1960] Ch 1).
- Only rights held as a member are enforceable. Outsider rights, such as a right to be the company's solicitor, are not (Eley v Positive Government Security Life Assurance (1876); Hickman v Kent or Romney Marsh Sheepbreeders' Association [1915] 1 Ch 881).
- Terms can be implied only where necessary to make the articles work (Attorney General of Belize v Belize Telecom [2009] UKPC 10; Marks & Spencer v BNP Paribas [2015] UKSC 72).
- A company cannot contract out of its statutory power to alter its articles, but members can bind themselves in a shareholders' agreement about how they will vote (Russell v Northern Bank Development Corp [1992] 1 WLR 588).

Capacity and authority
- Objects are unrestricted unless the articles restrict them (s.31), and a company's capacity cannot be challenged on the ground of anything in its constitution (s.39). This ended the ultra vires doctrine (Ashbury Railway Carriage v Riche (1875)).
- For a person dealing with the company in good faith, the directors' power to bind the company is deemed free of constitutional limits (s.40). Good faith is presumed, and merely knowing that an act is beyond the directors' powers is not bad faith (s.40(2)(b)).
- If the third party is a director or connected person, the transaction is voidable instead (s.41).

Illustration. Brook Ltd's articles cap borrowing at £50,000. The directors borrow £80,000 from a bank that has read the articles. The loan binds Brook Ltd under s.40, but the directors are liable to the company for breaching s.171.

Exam pitfalls:
- s.40 protects outsiders; it does not cure the directors' breach.
- A weighted-voting clause can protect a director from removal under s.168 (Bushell v Faith [1970] AC 1099).

The duties are codified but read in light of the old case law (s.170(3)–(4)). They are owed to the company, not to individual shareholders (s.170(1); Percival v Wright [1902] 2 Ch 421).

The duties
- s.171: act within the constitution and use powers only for their proper purposes. The court asks for what substantial purpose the power was used (Howard Smith v Ampol Petroleum [1974] AC 821). In Eclairs Group v JKX Oil & Gas [2015] UKSC 71 the board's power to restrict shares for non-disclosure (s.793 notices) was used to influence the outcome of a general meeting, an improper purpose. Lord Sumption (with Lord Hodge) proposed a "but for" test for mixed purposes, but Lord Mance and Lord Neuberger reserved the point, so the "primary or substantial purpose" test has not been displaced.
- s.172: act in the way the director considers, in good faith, would most likely promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, having regard to the s.172(1) factors such as employees, the community and environment, and long-term consequences ("enlightened shareholder value"). The test is subjective (Regentcrest plc v Cohen [2001] 2 BCLC 80); if the director never considered the company's interests, the court asks whether an intelligent, honest director could have thought it beneficial (Charterbridge Corp v Lloyds Bank [1970] Ch 62). Under BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA [2022] UKSC 25, creditors' interests must be considered once directors know or ought to know the company is insolvent or bordering on it, or that insolvent liquidation or administration is probable.
- s.173: exercise independent judgment. s.176: do not accept benefits from third parties.
- s.174: reasonable care, skill and diligence. The test is objective (what is reasonably expected of someone in the role), raised by the director's own knowledge and experience (Re D'Jan of London [1994] 1 BCLC 561).
- s.175: avoid conflicts of interest, including exploiting property, information or opportunities, whether or not the company could have used them (Regal (Hastings) Ltd v Gulliver [1967] 2 AC 134n; Industrial Development Consultants v Cooley [1972] 1 WLR 443; Bhullar v Bhullar [2003] EWCA Civ 424). Independent directors may authorise a conflict (s.175(4)–(6)); the duty survives resignation (s.170(2)).
- s.177: declare an interest in a proposed transaction with the company; existing transactions fall under s.182.

Remedies and relief
- Equitable remedies apply: account of profits, compensation, rescission (s.178).
- Ratification is by members' resolution, disregarding votes of the interested director and connected persons (s.239).
- Exemption clauses are void (s.232); the court may relieve an honest, reasonable director (s.1157).

Illustration. Dana, a director of Pipe Ltd, learns of a project while acting for Pipe. The client will not deal with Pipe, so Dana resigns and takes it herself. Like Cooley, she must account for her profit.

Exam pitfalls:
- s.175 is strict: good faith and the company's inability to exploit the opportunity are no defence.
- s.175 covers conflicts with third parties; s.177 covers transactions with the company itself.

The rule in Foss v Harbottle (1843) 2 Hare 461 has two limbs: for a wrong done to the company, the company is the proper claimant; and the court will not interfere with an irregularity that the majority could cure. Shareholders therefore use four main routes.

1. Personal claims. A member can enforce personal rights under the constitution (s.33; Pender v Lushington (1877) 6 Ch D 70). But a shareholder cannot recover a fall in share value or lost dividends that merely reflects loss suffered by the company (Prudential Assurance v Newman Industries (No 2) [1982] Ch 204; Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1). Sevilleja v Marex Financial Ltd [2020] UKSC 31 confined this reflective loss rule to shareholders; it does not bar creditors.

2. The statutory derivative claim (CA 2006 ss 260–264). A member may sue on the company's behalf for an actual or proposed negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust by a director (s.260(3)). Permission involves two stages.
- The claimant must show a prima facie case, or the claim is dismissed (s.261).
- Permission must be refused if a person acting under s.172 would not continue the claim, or if the conduct has been authorised or ratified (s.263(2)). Otherwise the court weighs the s.263(3) factors, such as good faith and any personal remedy, and must consider disinterested members' views (s.263(4)). See Iesini v Westrip Holdings [2009] EWHC 2526 (Ch).

3. Unfair prejudice (s.994). A member may petition where the company's affairs are conducted in a manner unfairly prejudicial to members' interests. Fairness is judged against the terms on which members agreed to associate, including informal understandings in a quasi-partnership (O'Neill v Phillips [1999] 1 WLR 1092). Typical cases are exclusion from management, diversion of business and excessive pay. The court may make any order it thinks fit (s.996), usually a purchase of the petitioner's shares, generally valued pro rata without a minority discount in a quasi-partnership (Re Bird Precision Bellows [1986] Ch 658).

4. Just and equitable winding up (Insolvency Act 1986 s.122(1)(g); Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries [1973] AC 360). It is a last resort, and may be refused where the petitioner unreasonably ignores another remedy (IA 1986 s.125(2)).

Illustration. Asha, Ben and Cal founded Dene Ltd as equal partners in all but name. Ben and Cal remove Asha as a director and stop her income. Her exclusion is unfairly prejudicial, unless they make a fair offer to buy her shares (O'Neill).

Exam pitfalls:
- s.994 is not a no-fault exit: a member cannot leave simply because trust has broken down (O'Neill).
- Check ratification: s.239 excludes the wrongdoer's votes, and ratification forces refusal under s.263(2).

The capital maintenance rules protect creditors by preventing capital being returned to members except through approved procedures (Trevor v Whitworth (1887) 12 App Cas 409).

Raising capital
- Private companies have no minimum capital. A public company needs allotted share capital of at least £50,000 nominal (s.763), with each share paid up to at least one-quarter of its nominal value plus the whole premium (s.586), before it gets a trading certificate (s.761).
- Shares may not be allotted at a discount to nominal value (s.580; Ooregum Gold Mining Co of India v Roper [1892] AC 125). Public companies need an independent valuation of non-cash consideration (s.593).
- Members have pre-emption rights on allotments of equity securities for cash (s.561), which can be disapplied.

Distributions
- Only profits available for the purpose may be distributed: accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses (s.830). Public companies must also satisfy the net assets test in s.831.
- A member who knew or had reasonable grounds to believe a distribution was unlawful must repay it (s.847); ignorance of the law is no excuse (It's a Wrap (UK) Ltd v Gula [2006] EWCA Civ 544). Directors who authorise it are liable for breach of duty.
- A disguised return, such as selling an asset to a shareholder at an undervalue, can be an unlawful distribution. Substance prevails (Aveling Barford v Perion [1989] BCLC 626). In Progress Property Co v Moorgarth Group [2010] UKSC 55 a sale genuinely believed to be at market value was not a distribution.

Reductions and buy-backs
- Capital can be reduced by special resolution confirmed by the court (ss 645–651) or, for private companies, by special resolution backed by a directors' solvency statement (ss 641–644).
- A company may not acquire its own shares except under Part 18 (s.658). Purchases must be funded from distributable profits or a fresh issue; private companies may use capital with a solvency statement, auditor's report and special resolution (ss 709–723).
- Financial assistance for acquiring a company's own shares is prohibited only for public companies, and for private subsidiaries assisting the acquisition of shares in a public parent (ss 678–679). The purpose exceptions are narrow (Brady v Brady [1989] AC 755).

Worked example. Kestrel Ltd has realised profits of £400,000, realised losses of £150,000 and an unrealised revaluation gain of £100,000. Distributable profits are £400,000 − £150,000 = £250,000; the revaluation gain is unrealised and excluded.

Exam pitfalls:
- The s.831 net assets test applies only to public companies.
- The financial assistance ban no longer applies to private companies generally.
- Nominal value is not market value, and a share premium is not distributable.

Corporate governance concerns how companies are directed and controlled. Its core problem is agency: once ownership separates from control, managers may serve themselves (Berle and Means 1932; Jensen and Meckling 1976).

Division of power
- Under the model articles the directors manage the business (art 3), subject to the members' reserve power to direct them by special resolution (art 4). Members cannot override the board by ordinary resolution (Automatic Self-Cleansing Filter Syndicate Co v Cuninghame [1906] 2 Ch 34).
- Members' key controls: removing a director by ordinary resolution on special notice (s.168), altering the articles (s.21), and approving long service contracts (s.188), substantial property transactions (s.190) and loans to directors (s.197).
- An ordinary resolution needs a simple majority (s.282); a special resolution at least 75% (s.283).

The UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
- Published by the FRC and applied through the FCA's UK Listing Rules to companies in the equity shares (commercial companies) category, for financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. Provision 29, a declaration on the effectiveness of material internal controls, applies from 1 January 2026.
- It operates on "comply or explain": companies report how they applied the Principles and either follow the Provisions or explain departures.
- Key Provisions: separate chair and chief executive; a chair independent on appointment; at least half the board, excluding the chair, independent non-executives; audit, remuneration and nomination committees; annual re-election of directors.
- Law adds a binding vote on directors' remuneration policy at least every three years (s.439A), an annual advisory vote on the remuneration report (s.439) and the s.172 statement for large companies (s.414CZA).

History: Cadbury (1992), Greenbury (1995), Hampel (1998), Higgs (2003), then the UK Code from 2010.

Attribution
- A company acts through people, and the rule for attributing acts and knowledge depends on the purpose of the rule being applied (Meridian Global Funds Management Asia v Securities Commission [1995] 2 AC 500).
- Traditionally, for crimes requiring a mental element, only the "directing mind and will" counted (Tesco Supermarkets v Nattrass [1972] AC 153). The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, s.196 (from 26 December 2023) made a company liable for a listed economic crime committed by a senior manager acting within their actual or apparent authority. The Crime and Policing Act 2026, s.250 extended this senior manager test to all offences from 29 June 2026, for offences committed on or after that date. Large organisations also face the failure to prevent fraud offence (s.199), in force since 1 September 2025.

Illustration. A listed company appoints its retiring chief executive as chair. This departs from the Code, but there is no breach of law: the company must give a clear explanation, which investors may reject when they vote.

Exam pitfalls:
- The Code is not law; departure is legitimate if explained.
- Distinguish shareholder primacy, enlightened shareholder value (s.172) and stakeholder theory.

notes.h: Sale of goods: passing of property, risk and title
notes.body:
The Sale of Goods Act 1979 covers transfers of property in goods for a money price (s.2(1)). Consumer sales fall mainly under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, but the SGA property rules still apply. Property matters for risk, the action for the price (s.49) and insolvency.

Specific and unascertained goods
- Specific goods are identified and agreed on at contract (s.61). Property in unascertained goods cannot pass until they are ascertained (s.16; Re Goldcorp Exchange [1995] 1 AC 74).
- Exception: a buyer who has paid for part of an identified bulk becomes an owner in common (ss 20A–20B).

Intention governs (s.17); s.18 supplies presumptions.
- Rule 1: in an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is later.
- Rules 2 and 3: if the seller must put specific goods into a deliverable state, or weigh or measure them to fix the price, property passes once done and the buyer has notice.
- Rule 4: on sale or return, property passes when the buyer approves or adopts the transaction or keeps them beyond the time allowed.
- Rule 5: for unascertained or future goods sold by description, property passes on unconditional appropriation of goods in a deliverable state with the other party's assent (Federspiel v Twigg [1957]). Delivery to a carrier usually suffices (r.5(2)).

Retention of title (s.19). A seller may keep ownership until paid (Aluminium Industrie Vaassen v Romalpa [1976] 1 WLR 676), even for all sums owed (Armour v Thyssen Edelstahlwerke [1991] 2 AC 339). Claims to new products or proceeds usually amount to unregistered charges and fail (Re Peachdart [1984] Ch 131). Unless property has passed, the seller can sue for the price only if it is payable on a day certain (s.49; FG Wilson v John Holt [2013] EWCA Civ 1232).

Risk passes with property (s.20(1)), but a party at fault for delay bears losses caused by it (s.20(2)). Consumer goods stay at the trader's risk until the consumer takes possession (CRA 2015 s.29).

Nemo dat (s.21). A buyer gets no better title than the seller had, except by estoppel, sale under a voidable title not yet avoided (s.23; Car & Universal Finance v Caldwell [1965] 1 QB 525), seller in possession (s.24), buyer in possession (s.25), mercantile agents (Factors Act 1889 s.2) and private buyers of motor vehicles on hire purchase (Hire Purchase Act 1964 Pt III). In Shogun Finance v Hudson [2003] UKHL 62 a written contract naming the impersonated person was void, so s.23 could not apply.

Exam pitfalls:
- Check s.17 intention first, then classify the goods before choosing a s.18 rule.

Agency arises when a principal (P) authorises an agent (A) to affect P's legal relations with third parties (T). The central question is usually whether A had authority to bind P.

Actual authority
- Express or implied from the agent's role or a course of dealing (Hely-Hutchinson v Brayhead Ltd [1968] 1 QB 549). It arises from the P–A agreement; T need not know of it.

Apparent (ostensible) authority
- It arises where P represents to T that A has authority, T relies on that, and T alters position (Freeman & Lockyer v Buckhurst Park Properties [1964] 2 QB 480, Diplock LJ).
- The representation must come from P or someone with actual authority, not from A alone (Armagas v Mundogas (The Ocean Frost) [1986] AC 717), though A may have apparent authority to communicate P's approval (First Energy (UK) v Hungarian International Bank [1993] 2 Lloyd's Rep 194).
- T cannot rely on it if T knew, or was put on inquiry, that A lacked authority.

Ratification
- P may adopt an unauthorised act retrospectively (Bolton Partners v Lambert (1889) 41 Ch D 295), but A must have purported to act for P (Keighley, Maxsted & Co v Durant [1901] AC 240), P must have existed when A acted (Kelner v Baxter (1866); CA 2006 s.51) and ratification must be timely.

Undisclosed principal. P can sue and be sued on contracts A makes within actual authority, unless the contract excludes this or T had a good reason to refuse to deal with P (Siu Yin Kwan v Eastern Insurance [1994] 2 AC 199).

Agent's duties: obey, use care, avoid conflicts, make no secret profit. Bribes are held on constructive trust for P (FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital Partners [2014] UKSC 45).

Agent's own liability. A is usually not a party to the contract, but if A lacks authority A is strictly liable to T for breach of warranty of authority (Collen v Wright (1857); Yonge v Toynbee [1910] 1 KB 215).

Commercial agents. Self-employed agents negotiating sales or purchases of goods are protected by the Commercial Agents (Council Directive) Regulations 1993: minimum notice and compensation or indemnity on termination (regs 15–18). Compensation reflects the value of the agency at termination (Lonsdale v Howard & Hallam [2007] UKHL 32).

Illustration. Fern, a junior buyer, orders £200,000 of steel. Her limit is £50,000, but her manager had told the supplier that Fern "handles all steel purchasing". The manager's statement can give her apparent authority.

Exam pitfalls:
- Keep actual and apparent authority separate.
- An agent cannot "self-authorise" (The Ocean Frost).
- An undisclosed principal cannot ratify.

cards.f: What did Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] establish?
cards.b: A properly registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when one person holds almost all the shares. Mr Salomon was not personally liable for the company's debts and could rank as a secured creditor.

cards.f: Which section of CA 2006 confers corporate personality on registration?
cards.b: Section 16: on registration the subscribers and later members become a body corporate under the registered name.

cards.f: Lee v Lee's Air Farming Ltd [1961]: what was the point?
cards.b: A controlling shareholder and director can also be an employee under a contract with his own company, so his widow could claim compensation as the widow of a worker.

cards.f: Why did the claim fail in Macaura v Northern Assurance [1925]?
cards.b: Macaura had transferred his timber to a company he owned and then insured it in his own name. As a shareholder he had no insurable interest in the company's property.

cards.f: State the evasion principle from Prest v Petrodel [2013].
cards.b: The veil may be pierced where a person under an existing legal obligation or restriction deliberately evades it, or frustrates its enforcement, by interposing a company under their control. The court then removes only the advantage gained.

cards.f: How does the concealment principle differ from evasion (Prest)?
cards.b: Concealment means the company hides the identity of the real actors; the court simply looks behind it to find the facts. That is not piercing. Evasion involves using the company to escape an existing obligation, and only then is the veil truly pierced.

cards.f: Gilford Motor Co v Horne [1933] in one sentence.
cards.b: A former employee bound by a non-solicitation covenant set up a company to solicit customers; an injunction was granted against both him and the company because the company was a device to evade his obligation.

cards.f: What did Adams v Cape Industries [1990] decide about corporate groups?
cards.b: There is no general single economic unit doctrine and no piercing just because justice requires it. Using a group structure so that future liabilities fall on particular subsidiaries is a legitimate use of incorporation.

cards.f: How did Vedanta v Lungowe [2019] treat parent company liability?
cards.b: A parent can owe a direct duty of care in negligence to people harmed by a subsidiary's operations, for example where it controls those operations or issues group-wide policies and holds itself out as ensuring they are implemented. This is ordinary tort law, not veil piercing.

cards.f: Why was the veil not pierced in Prest itself, and how did the wife succeed?
cards.b: The husband was not evading any existing obligation by holding properties through his companies, so piercing was unavailable. The wife succeeded because, on the facts, the companies held the properties on resulting trust for the husband.

cards.f: Name two statutory provisions that can make individuals liable for a company's debts.
cards.b: Wrongful trading (Insolvency Act 1986 s.214) and fraudulent trading (IA 1986 s.213). Section 216 (re-use of a prohibited company name) is another example.

cards.f: What does a company's constitution include under CA 2006 s.17?
cards.b: The articles of association and the resolutions and agreements to which s.29 applies, such as special resolutions.

cards.f: What majority is needed to alter the articles?
cards.b: A special resolution, passed by at least 75% of the votes cast (ss 21 and 283).

cards.f: What does s.33 CA 2006 do?
cards.b: It makes the constitution binding between the company and its members as if each had covenanted to observe it, creating a statutory contract enforceable by and against members.

cards.f: Explain the outsider rights problem with Eley v Positive Government Security Life Assurance (1876).
cards.b: The articles named Eley as the company's solicitor for life. He could not enforce this because s.33 rights are enforceable only by members in their capacity as members, not in some outside role.

cards.f: What test applies to an alteration of articles (Allen v Gold Reefs [1900])?
cards.b: The power must be exercised bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole. Courts defer to the shareholders' honest judgment unless no reasonable shareholder could consider the change beneficial.

cards.f: What is the effect of s.39 CA 2006?
cards.b: A company's capacity cannot be called into question on the ground of lack of capacity because of anything in its constitution, effectively abolishing ultra vires as against outsiders.

cards.f: How does s.40 CA 2006 protect third parties?
cards.b: In favour of a person dealing with the company in good faith, the directors' power to bind the company, or authorise others, is deemed free of any limitation under the constitution. Good faith is presumed, and mere knowledge that an act exceeds the directors' powers is not bad faith.

cards.f: When does s.41 apply instead of s.40?
cards.b: Where the other party is a director of the company or its holding company, or a person connected with such a director. The transaction is then voidable at the company's instance.

cards.f: What did Russell v Northern Bank Development Corp [1992] decide?
cards.b: A company cannot fetter its statutory power to alter its articles, but shareholders may validly agree among themselves, in a shareholders' agreement, how they will vote.

cards.f: What was held in Bushell v Faith [1970]?
cards.b: A clause giving a director weighted votes on a resolution to remove him was valid, so he could defeat removal under what is now s.168. Such clauses are common in small private companies.

cards.f: Are objects clauses still required?
cards.b: No. Under s.31 a company's objects are unrestricted unless its articles specifically restrict them.

cards.f: To whom are directors' general duties owed?
cards.b: To the company (s.170(1)), not to individual shareholders or creditors. Percival v Wright [1902] confirms no general duty to individual members.

cards.f: List the seven general duties in CA 2006.
cards.b: s.171 act within powers; s.172 promote the success of the company; s.173 independent judgment; s.174 care, skill and diligence; s.175 avoid conflicts; s.176 no third-party benefits; s.177 declare interest in proposed transactions.

cards.f: Is the s.172 test objective or subjective?
cards.b: Mainly subjective: the question is what the director honestly considered would promote the company's success (Regentcrest v Cohen [2001]). If the director never considered the company's interests, the court asks what an intelligent and honest director could have believed (Charterbridge).

cards.f: What is the s.174 standard of care?
cards.b: Objective minimum: the knowledge, skill and experience reasonably expected of a person carrying out the director's functions. Subjective uplift: the director's own general knowledge, skill and experience, if greater.

cards.f: Howard Smith v Ampol Petroleum [1974]: key principle.
cards.b: Directors issued shares to destroy a majority bloc and enable a takeover. The power to issue shares was used for an improper substantial purpose, so the issue was set aside even though directors were not acting for personal gain.

cards.f: When must directors consider creditors' interests (BTI v Sequana [2022])?
cards.b: When they know or ought to know that the company is insolvent or bordering on insolvency, or that an insolvent liquidation or administration is probable. The weight given to creditors increases as the company's position worsens.

cards.f: Regal (Hastings) v Gulliver: why were the directors liable?
cards.b: They profited from shares they acquired because of their position as directors. Liability to account was strict despite their good faith and the company's inability to buy the shares itself.

cards.f: How does s.175 deal with conflicts that the board authorises?
cards.b: For a private company, independent directors can authorise a conflict unless the constitution forbids it; for a public company the constitution must expressly permit it. The interested director's vote and quorum count are disregarded.

cards.f: Distinguish s.175 from s.177.
cards.b: s.175 covers situations of conflict with the company's interests, such as exploiting opportunities. s.177 applies where a director is interested in a proposed transaction with the company itself and requires declaration to the other directors.

cards.f: How does ratification work under s.239?
cards.b: The company may ratify by members' resolution, but votes of the director concerned and persons connected with him are disregarded. Some acts, such as fraud on the minority, may be unratifiable.

cards.f: What does s.232 CA 2006 do?
cards.b: It makes void any provision exempting a director from liability for negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust towards the company, subject to permitted insurance and indemnities.

cards.f: State the two limbs of Foss v Harbottle (1843).
cards.b: The proper claimant principle: for a wrong done to the company, only the company can sue. The majority rule principle: the court will not intervene in internal irregularities that the majority could ratify.

cards.f: What can found a statutory derivative claim under s.260(3)?
cards.b: An actual or proposed act or omission involving negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust by a director. The claim may be brought against the director or another person.

cards.f: When must the court refuse permission for a derivative claim?
cards.b: Under s.263(2): if a person acting under s.172 would not seek to continue the claim, or if the act or omission has been authorised or ratified by the company.

cards.f: What is the reflective loss rule?
cards.b: A shareholder cannot recover a drop in share value or distributions that merely reflects loss suffered by the company, where the company has its own cause of action (Prudential v Newman; Johnson v Gore Wood).

cards.f: How did Sevilleja v Marex [2020] change the reflective loss rule?
cards.b: The Supreme Court confined it to claims by shareholders, in that capacity, for a fall in share value or distributions. It does not apply to creditors, even if they are also shareholders claiming as creditors.

cards.f: What must a petitioner show under s.994?
cards.b: That the company's affairs are being or have been conducted in a manner unfairly prejudicial to the interests of members generally or some members, including the petitioner, or that an actual or proposed act or omission would be so.

cards.f: What did O'Neill v Phillips [1999] say about fairness?
cards.b: Fairness is judged against the agreed basis of association, including equitable considerations such as informal understandings in a quasi-partnership. There is no right to exit merely because trust has broken down.

cards.f: What is the usual remedy under s.996?
cards.b: An order that the respondents buy the petitioner's shares at a fair value, typically pro rata with no minority discount where the company is a quasi-partnership.

cards.f: What is a quasi-partnership (Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries [1973])?
cards.b: A company formed on personal relationships of mutual confidence, usually with an understanding that all or some members will participate in management and with restrictions on share transfer.

cards.f: Why might a just and equitable winding up petition be refused?
cards.b: The court may refuse if some other remedy is available and the petitioner is acting unreasonably in pursuing winding up instead (IA 1986 s.125(2)), for example after refusing a fair buy-out offer.

cards.f: What is the minimum share capital for a public company?
cards.b: £50,000 nominal value of allotted share capital (s.763), with each share at least one-quarter paid up plus the whole of any premium (s.586).

cards.f: Can shares be allotted at a discount?
cards.b: No. Shares may not be allotted for less than their nominal value (s.580; Ooregum Gold Mining v Roper [1892]). The allottee is liable to pay the discount plus interest.

cards.f: Define distributable profits under s.830.
cards.b: Accumulated realised profits, so far as not previously used by distribution or capitalisation, less accumulated realised losses, so far as not previously written off in a reduction or reorganisation of capital.

cards.f: What extra test applies to public company distributions (s.831)?
cards.b: The distribution must not reduce net assets below the total of called-up share capital and undistributable reserves.

cards.f: When must a shareholder repay an unlawful distribution?
cards.b: Under s.847, if at the time of the distribution the shareholder knew or had reasonable grounds to believe it was unlawful. Knowledge of the facts suffices; ignorance of the law is no defence (It's a Wrap v Gula [2006]).

cards.f: What was decided in Aveling Barford v Perion [1989]?
cards.b: A sale of property at a gross undervalue to a company controlled by the shareholder was an unlawful return of capital, because the company had no distributable profits. Courts look at substance, not labels.

cards.f: How did Progress Property v Moorgarth [2010] refine Aveling Barford?
cards.b: Whether a transaction is a disguised distribution depends on its real nature. A sale genuinely believed by the directors to be at arm's length and at fair value was not a distribution, even though the price turned out too low.

cards.f: How can a private company reduce its capital without court approval?
cards.b: By special resolution supported by a solvency statement made by all the directors (ss 641–644).

cards.f: Does the financial assistance ban apply to private companies?
cards.b: Generally not since CA 2006. It applies to public companies and to a private subsidiary giving assistance for the acquisition of shares in its public holding company (ss 678–679).

cards.f: Is a share premium account distributable?
cards.b: No. Share premium must be credited to a share premium account and is treated as capital, though it may be used for limited purposes such as paying up bonus shares or issue expenses (s.610).

cards.f: What is the agency problem in corporate governance?
cards.b: When ownership is separated from control, managers (agents) may act in their own interests rather than those of the shareholders (principals). Governance mechanisms aim to reduce these agency costs.

cards.f: What does 'comply or explain' mean?
cards.b: Companies subject to the UK Corporate Governance Code must report how they applied its Principles and either comply with each Provision or explain why they have not.

cards.f: Which companies must report against the UK Corporate Governance Code 2024?
cards.b: Companies with a listing in the equity shares (commercial companies) category, through the FCA's UK Listing Rules. It applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2025, with Provision 29 from 1 January 2026.

cards.f: What is Provision 29 of the 2024 Code?
cards.b: The board must declare in the annual report whether its material internal controls were effective at the balance sheet date, and describe any that were not.

cards.f: How can members remove a director?
cards.b: By ordinary resolution at a meeting under s.168, with special notice (28 days) and a right for the director to protest. A written resolution cannot be used.

cards.f: What did Automatic Self-Cleansing Filter Syndicate v Cuninghame [1906] decide?
cards.b: Where the articles give management powers to the board, the members cannot override the directors' decisions by ordinary resolution; they must alter the articles or remove directors.

cards.f: What votes do shareholders of quoted companies have on directors' pay?
cards.b: A binding vote on the remuneration policy at least every three years (s.439A) and an annual advisory vote on the directors' remuneration report (s.439).

cards.f: State the Meridian [1995] approach to attribution.
cards.b: Whose acts or knowledge count as the company's depends on interpreting the particular rule in question, including its language, content and policy, rather than always applying the directing mind test.

cards.f: What did s.196 Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 change?
cards.b: For listed economic crimes such as fraud and bribery, a body corporate is guilty if a senior manager acting within actual or apparent authority commits the offence, extending beyond the narrow Tesco v Nattrass directing mind test. The Crime and Policing Act 2026 (s.250, in force 29 June 2026) extended the senior manager test to all offences.

cards.f: Name three key UK governance reports before the 2010 Code.
cards.b: Cadbury (1992) on board structure, Greenbury (1995) on remuneration and Higgs (2003) on non-executive directors. Hampel (1998) and Walker (2009) are also important.

cards.f: Contrast shareholder primacy with stakeholder theory.
cards.b: Shareholder primacy holds that the company should be run to maximise shareholder value. Stakeholder theory says boards should balance the interests of all groups affected. s.172 takes a middle path: enlightened shareholder value.

cards.f: What is the basic rule for when property passes under SGA 1979?
cards.b: Property passes when the parties intend it to pass (s.17). The s.18 rules apply only where no different intention appears.

cards.f: State s.16 SGA 1979.
cards.b: Where there is a contract for the sale of unascertained goods, no property passes to the buyer unless and until the goods are ascertained.

cards.f: Explain s.18 Rule 1.
cards.b: In an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, property passes when the contract is made, regardless of whether payment or delivery is postponed.

cards.f: When does property pass on sale or return (Rule 4)?
cards.b: When the buyer signifies approval or acceptance or does any act adopting the transaction, or keeps the goods beyond the agreed time or, if none, a reasonable time without giving notice of rejection.

cards.f: What is unconditional appropriation under Rule 5?
cards.b: An irrevocable attachment of specific goods to the contract, with the express or implied assent of the other party, so that the seller can no longer substitute other goods. Delivery to a carrier without reserving the right of disposal usually suffices.

cards.f: When does risk pass under SGA 1979?
cards.b: Prima facie risk passes with property (s.20(1)), but where delivery is delayed through either party's fault, that party bears any loss that might not otherwise have occurred (s.20(2)).

cards.f: How does the Consumer Rights Act 2015 alter risk?
cards.b: Under s.29, goods remain at the trader's risk until they come into the physical possession of the consumer or a person identified by the consumer, unless the consumer's own chosen carrier is used.

cards.f: What do ss 20A–20B SGA add for bulk goods?
cards.b: A buyer who has paid for some or all of a specified quantity of goods forming part of an identified bulk becomes an owner in common of the bulk, sharing proportionately.

cards.f: Why do extended retention of title clauses often fail?
cards.b: Clauses claiming new products made from the goods, or the proceeds of resale, are usually construed as creating charges by way of security, which are void against a liquidator or administrator if not registered (Re Peachdart [1984]).

cards.f: State the nemo dat rule and its statutory source.
cards.b: A buyer acquires no better title than the seller had (s.21 SGA 1979), subject to exceptions such as estoppel, voidable title (s.23), seller in possession (s.24) and buyer in possession (s.25).

cards.f: How did Car & Universal Finance v Caldwell [1965] apply s.23?
cards.b: The owner avoided the rogue's voidable title by informing the police and the AA, since the rogue could not be found. So the rogue had no title to pass when he sold on.

cards.f: Define actual authority.
cards.b: Authority that the principal has given the agent by agreement, either expressly or impliedly. It is a legal relationship between principal and agent alone.

cards.f: What are the elements of apparent authority (Freeman & Lockyer [1964])?
cards.b: A representation by the principal that the agent has authority, reliance by the third party on that representation, and an alteration of position by the third party.

cards.f: Can an agent create their own apparent authority?
cards.b: No. The representation must come from the principal or someone with actual authority (Armagas v Mundogas, The Ocean Frost [1986]).

cards.f: What did First Energy v Hungarian International Bank [1993] add?
cards.b: An agent who lacked apparent authority to make a deal may still have apparent authority to tell the third party that head office has approved it, binding the principal.

cards.f: List the conditions for ratification.
cards.b: The agent must have purported to act for the principal; the principal must have existed and had capacity when the act was done; and the principal must ratify the whole act with knowledge of the material facts, within a reasonable time.

cards.f: Why can't an undisclosed principal ratify?
cards.b: Because the agent did not purport to act on anyone's behalf (Keighley, Maxsted & Co v Durant [1901]).

cards.f: What is breach of warranty of authority?
cards.b: An agent who represents that they have authority they lack is strictly liable to the third party for loss caused (Collen v Wright (1857)), even if they honestly believed they had authority (Yonge v Toynbee [1910]).

cards.f: What remedy did FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital [2014] confirm for bribes?
cards.b: A bribe or secret commission received by an agent is held on constructive trust for the principal, giving the principal a proprietary claim.

cards.f: When can an undisclosed principal not intervene?
cards.b: When the contract expressly or impliedly excludes it, or where the identity of the contracting party is important to the third party (Siu Yin Kwan v Eastern Insurance [1994]).

cards.f: What do the Commercial Agents Regulations 1993 provide on termination?
cards.b: Minimum notice periods (reg 15) and a right to compensation, or to an indemnity if the contract provides for it (regs 17–18). Compensation reflects the market value of the agency at termination (Lonsdale v Howard & Hallam [2007]).

cards.f: What does s.51 CA 2006 say about pre-incorporation contracts?
cards.b: A contract made on behalf of a company not yet formed takes effect as one made with the person acting for it, who is personally liable, subject to any agreement to the contrary. The company cannot ratify it once formed.

questions.q: Which case established that a duly registered company is a legal person separate from its members?
options: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897]
Foss v Harbottle (1843)
Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd [2013]
Adams v Cape Industries plc [1990]
questions.why: Salomon is the foundation of separate legal personality. Prest and Adams concern the limits of piercing the veil; Foss concerns minority actions.

questions.q: A special resolution to alter a company's articles requires:
options: A simple majority of members present
At least 75% of the votes cast
At least 90% of the votes cast
Unanimous written consent
questions.why: Articles are altered by special resolution under s.21, which s.283 defines as a majority of not less than 75%.

questions.q: Under CA 2006 s.174, a director's standard of care is:
options: Purely subjective, based on the director's own skill
Purely objective, based on a reasonable director
Objective, raised if the director has greater personal knowledge, skill and experience
Gross negligence only, following Re City Equitable Fire Insurance
questions.why: s.174(2) sets an objective minimum for someone in the role, plus a subjective uplift for the director's own attributes, as in Re D'Jan.

questions.q: Which of the following must lead the court to refuse permission to continue a derivative claim?
options: The claimant holds less than 5% of the shares
The company has decided not to pursue the claim
The breach of duty has been ratified by the company
The claimant has a possible claim under s.994
questions.why: Ratification or authorisation is a mandatory bar under s.263(2)(c). The company's decision not to sue and alternative remedies are only discretionary factors under s.263(3).

questions.q: Kite Ltd, a private company, has accumulated realised profits of £300,000, accumulated realised losses of £120,000 and an unrealised revaluation surplus of £80,000. What is the maximum lawful dividend?
questions.why: Under s.830, distributable profits are realised profits less realised losses: £300,000 − £120,000 = £180,000. The unrealised surplus is excluded.

questions.q: The UK Corporate Governance Code operates on which basis?
options: Strict legal obligation enforceable by the FRC
Comply or explain
Voluntary disclosure with no reporting requirement
Apply and explain
questions.why: Companies in scope must state how they applied the Principles and comply with the Provisions or explain departures. 'Apply and explain' is the Wates Principles approach for large private companies.

questions.q: Under SGA 1979 s.18 Rule 1, property in specific goods in a deliverable state under an unconditional contract passes:
options: On delivery
On payment
When the contract is made
When the buyer accepts the goods
questions.why: Rule 1 passes property at the time of contract, even if payment or delivery is postponed, unless a different intention appears (s.17).

questions.q: In Armagas v Mundogas (The Ocean Frost) [1986], the principal was not bound because:
options: The agent acted fraudulently
The only representation of authority came from the agent himself
The contract was outside the principal's capacity
The third party failed to ask for written confirmation
questions.why: Apparent authority requires a representation by the principal. An agent who lacks authority cannot create it by his own statements.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the law after Prest v Petrodel [2013]?
options: The veil may be pierced whenever justice requires it
The veil may be pierced only where a person deliberately evades an existing legal obligation through a company they control
The veil is pierced whenever a company is a wholly owned subsidiary
Piercing has been abolished in England and Wales
questions.why: Lord Sumption limited piercing to the evasion principle, applied as a last resort. Adams v Cape had already rejected piercing simply because justice requires it.

questions.q: Rook Ltd supplies yarn to Weaver Ltd under a clause reserving title to the yarn and to any cloth made from it until payment. Weaver Ltd enters administration owing for yarn that is now woven into cloth. The clause as regards the cloth most likely:
options: Gives Rook Ltd full ownership of the cloth
Creates a charge that is void against the administrator if unregistered
Is valid because the yarn can be traced into the cloth
Makes Rook Ltd a secured creditor whether or not registered
questions.why: Where goods lose their identity in a new product, a claim to the product is usually construed as a charge granted by the buyer (Re Peachdart; Borden v Scottish Timber), which is void against an administrator if not registered.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the 'concealment' and 'evasion' principles identified by Lord Sumption in Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd [2013].
markScheme: Concealment: company used to hide the identity of the real actors
Under concealment the court merely looks behind the company to establish facts; this is not true piercing
Evasion: person under an existing legal obligation deliberately evades it by interposing a company they control
Under evasion the court may pierce the veil, only to deprive the controller of the advantage and only if no other remedy exists
questions.modelAnswer: In Prest Lord Sumption separated two ideas. Concealment occurs where a company is used to hide who the real actors are. The court can simply look behind the corporate structure to discover the facts; legal personality is not disregarded. Evasion arises where someone already under a legal obligation or restriction deliberately avoids it, or frustrates its enforcement, by interposing a company under their control. Only then may the court pierce the veil, and only to remove the advantage obtained and where no other remedy is adequate.

questions.q: Explain the limits on enforcing the articles of association under CA 2006 s.33.
markScheme: s.33 makes the constitution a statutory contract binding the company and members
Members may enforce membership rights against the company and each other (Rayfield v Hands)
Outsider rights, such as a role as solicitor or director, are not enforceable (Eley; Hickman)
The contract is subject to alteration by special resolution and cannot be rectified; terms implied only if necessary
questions.modelAnswer: Section 33 treats the constitution as if each member and the company had covenanted to observe it, so a member can enforce rights such as voting or pre-emption against the company and, as in Rayfield v Hands, against other members. However, only rights held as a member are enforceable. In Eley the articles promised that a named member would be the company's solicitor, but this was an outsider right that s.33 did not protect (Hickman). The s.33 contract is also unusual because it can be changed by special resolution, it cannot be rectified, and terms are implied only where necessary.

questions.q: Outline the key elements of the duty in CA 2006 s.172 and explain the effect of BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA [2022].
markScheme: Duty to act in the way the director considers in good faith most likely to promote the success of the company for members as a whole
Must have regard to listed factors such as long-term consequences, employees, community and environment and reputation
Test is subjective (Regentcrest v Cohen), with Charterbridge test where the director never considered the issue
Sequana: creditor interests must be considered when directors know or ought to know of insolvency, near insolvency or probable insolvent liquidation or administration
The weight given to creditors' interests grows with the seriousness of the company's financial difficulties
questions.modelAnswer: Section 172 requires a director to act in the way he considers, in good faith, would be most likely to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, having regard to factors such as long-term consequences, employees, the community and environment, and reputation. The test is subjective (Regentcrest v Cohen). In Sequana the Supreme Court held that s.172(3) brings in a duty to consider creditors' interests when directors know or ought to know the company is insolvent or bordering on insolvency, or that insolvent liquidation or administration is probable. Creditors' interests weigh more heavily the worse the position becomes.

questions.q: What is the rule against reflective loss, and how was it limited in Sevilleja v Marex Financial Ltd [2020]?
markScheme: A shareholder cannot recover a fall in share value or distributions that reflects loss suffered by the company
The company is the proper claimant (Prudential v Newman; Johnson v Gore Wood)
Marex confined the rule to shareholder claims in that capacity; it does not bar creditors' claims
questions.modelAnswer: Where a company has a cause of action for a loss, a shareholder cannot sue for the consequent fall in the value of shares or dividends, because that loss merely reflects the company's loss and the company is the proper claimant (Prudential v Newman; Johnson v Gore Wood). In Marex the Supreme Court held the rule is a narrow rule of company law confined to shareholders claiming in that capacity. It does not prevent creditors, including those who are also shareholders but claim as creditors, from recovering their own losses.

questions.q: Explain when a transaction between a company and its shareholder may amount to an unlawful distribution, with reference to case law.
markScheme: A distribution includes every transfer of a company's assets to members, in cash or otherwise (s.829)
Courts look at substance rather than form (Aveling Barford v Perion)
Sale at a known undervalue to a shareholder-controlled company without distributable profits was unlawful (Aveling Barford)
A genuine arm's-length transaction honestly believed to be at fair value is not a distribution (Progress Property v Moorgarth)
questions.modelAnswer: Under s.829 a distribution covers any transfer of company assets to members, so it is not limited to declared dividends. The courts examine the real substance of a transaction. In Aveling Barford v Perion a property sold at a large undervalue to a company controlled by the sole shareholder was treated as a disguised return of capital and was unlawful because there were no distributable profits. In Progress Property v Moorgarth the Supreme Court clarified that the test depends on the real nature of the transaction: a sale the directors genuinely believed was at arm's length and at fair value was not a distribution even though the price turned out too low.

questions.q: State two ways in which shareholders can hold directors of a listed company to account.
markScheme: Removal by ordinary resolution under s.168 (or annual re-election under the Code)
Votes on remuneration: binding policy vote (s.439A) and advisory report vote (s.439)
questions.modelAnswer: Shareholders can remove any director by ordinary resolution with special notice under s.168, and under the UK Corporate Governance Code all directors of in-scope companies should stand for annual re-election. Shareholders of quoted companies also vote on directors' pay: a binding vote on the remuneration policy at least every three years under s.439A and an annual advisory vote on the remuneration report under s.439.

questions.q: Explain how s.18 Rule 5 SGA 1979 determines when property passes in unascertained goods.
markScheme: Applies to unascertained or future goods sold by description
Property passes when goods of the contract description in a deliverable state are unconditionally appropriated to the contract
Appropriation must be by one party with the express or implied assent of the other
Delivery to a carrier without reserving a right of disposal is usually an appropriation (r.5(2)); s.16 means nothing passes before ascertainment
questions.modelAnswer: Rule 5 covers contracts for unascertained or future goods sold by description. Because of s.16, property cannot pass until the goods are ascertained. It passes when goods of the right description and in a deliverable state are unconditionally appropriated to the contract by one party with the express or implied assent of the other. Appropriation means an irrevocable earmarking so that the seller can no longer substitute other goods (Federspiel v Twigg). Under r.5(2), delivering the goods to a carrier for transmission to the buyer, without reserving a right of disposal, is usually treated as unconditional appropriation.

questions.q: What conditions must be satisfied before a principal can ratify an agent's unauthorised contract?
markScheme: Agent purported to act on behalf of a named or identifiable principal (Keighley, Maxsted v Durant)
Principal existed and had capacity when the act was done (Kelner v Baxter)
Principal ratifies the whole contract with full knowledge, within a reasonable time
questions.modelAnswer: First, the agent must have purported to act on behalf of the principal; an undisclosed principal cannot ratify (Keighley, Maxsted v Durant). Second, the principal must have been in existence and had capacity at the time of the act, which is why a company cannot ratify a pre-incorporation contract (Kelner v Baxter; now s.51 CA 2006). Third, the principal must ratify the whole transaction with knowledge of the material facts and within a reasonable time, and ratification cannot unfairly prejudice third parties' accrued rights.

questions.q: Explain why the no-conflict rule is described as strict, using Regal (Hastings) v Gulliver and Bhullar v Bhullar.
markScheme: Liability does not depend on bad faith or loss to the company
Regal: directors liable despite honesty and the company's inability to take up the shares
Bhullar: opportunity falling within the company's line of business; reasonable person would see a real possibility of conflict
s.175(2) codifies that it is immaterial whether the company could take advantage of the opportunity
questions.modelAnswer: The no-conflict rule is strict because a director must account even if acting honestly and causing no loss. In Regal the directors bought shares when the company could not afford them, yet had to account because the opportunity came to them as directors. In Bhullar directors who bought land next to the company's property were liable because a reasonable person would see a real possibility of conflict; the opportunity was one the company would have been interested in. Section 175(2) codifies this: it is immaterial whether the company could take advantage of the property, information or opportunity.

questions.q: Hawk plc has called-up share capital of £1m, a share premium account of £200,000 and net assets of £1.35m. Its accumulated realised profits less realised losses are £250,000, and it has unrealised losses of £100,000. Calculate the maximum lawful dividend and explain.
markScheme: s.830: distributable profits are £250,000
s.831 applies because Hawk is a public company
Undistributable reserves include share premium: capital £1m + £200,000 = £1.2m
Net assets after distribution must not fall below £1.2m
Net asset headroom: £1.35m − £1.2m = £150,000
Maximum dividend is the lower figure: £150,000
questions.modelAnswer: Under s.830 Hawk's distributable profits are £250,000. As a public company it must also meet the net assets test in s.831: after the distribution, net assets must not be less than the total of called-up share capital and undistributable reserves. Share premium is an undistributable reserve, so the floor is £1,000,000 + £200,000 = £1,200,000. Net assets are £1,350,000, giving headroom of £150,000. The maximum lawful dividend is the lower of the two limits, £150,000.

questions.q: Mira owns 100% of Lantern Ltd, which owns 100% of Spark Ltd. Spark Ltd operates a battery recycling plant using a safety manual written by Lantern Ltd's group health and safety team, which also audits the plant every year. Toxic fumes from the plant injure nearby residents, including Jo. Spark Ltd has few assets. Separately, Mira sold her own recycling consultancy to Gale Ltd last year with a covenant not to compete in the North West for two years; she now trades in the North West through Ember Ltd, a company she set up and controls. Advise Jo and Gale Ltd.
markScheme: Separate personality: Spark Ltd, Lantern Ltd and Mira are distinct persons (Salomon; s.16)
No single economic unit doctrine in groups (Adams v Cape)
Jo cannot pierce the veil: no evasion of an existing obligation (Prest)
Jo's better route is a direct negligence claim against Lantern (Chandler v Cape; Vedanta; Okpabi)
Group-wide safety manual and annual audits may show Lantern assumed responsibility or held itself out as supervising
Need for proximity and foreseeability; outcome depends on the evidence of control
Gale: Mira was under an existing covenant and used Ember to evade it (Gilford v Horne; Jones v Lipman)
Remedy: injunction against Mira and Ember; piercing only to the extent needed and as a last resort (Prest)
Alternatively, the covenant may be enforced directly because Mira is acting through Ember, without needing to pierce
questions.modelAnswer:
Jo. Spark Ltd is a separate legal person and is primarily liable to Jo in negligence and possibly nuisance, but it has few assets. Lantern Ltd and Mira are distinct persons (Salomon; CA 2006 s.16), and English law does not treat a group as a single economic unit (Adams v Cape). Jo cannot pierce the veil: under Prest the evasion principle requires a pre-existing obligation that is deliberately evaded, and setting up a subsidiary to run a plant is not that.

Jo's stronger claim is against Lantern Ltd directly. Vedanta v Lungowe and Okpabi v Shell confirm that a parent may owe its own duty of care where it has taken over or shared management of the relevant activity, or issued group-wide policies and actively ensured their implementation. Here Lantern wrote the safety manual and audits the plant annually, which suggests it assumed responsibility for safety, as in Chandler v Cape. Jo must also prove foreseeability, proximity, breach and causation. If proven, Lantern is liable for its own negligence, not because the veil is lifted. Mira personally is unlikely to be liable unless she personally assumed responsibility.

Gale Ltd. Mira was under an existing contractual restriction and has interposed Ember Ltd, a company she controls, to carry on the competing business. This mirrors Gilford Motor v Horne and Jones v Lipman and falls within Lord Sumption's evasion principle. Gale can seek an injunction against Mira and also against Ember. Prest stresses that piercing is a last resort; the court may achieve the result simply by holding that Mira is in breach because she is competing through her company, and joining Ember as the instrument of the breach. Either way Gale should obtain relief, plus damages or an account for losses already suffered.

questions.q: Thorn Ltd's articles provide that (i) the company may not borrow more than £100,000 without a special resolution, and (ii) Ula will be the company's accountant for life. The directors borrow £250,000 from Vale Bank, whose manager read the articles but was told by the finance director that a special resolution had been passed. It had not. The members later pass a special resolution removing article (ii), and the board appoints a new accountant. Ula, who holds 5% of the shares, wishes to challenge her removal. Advise the parties.
markScheme: Borrowing limit is a constitutional limitation on directors' powers, not on capacity (s.39; s.31)
s.40: in favour of a person dealing in good faith, directors' power is deemed free of constitutional limits
Good faith presumed; knowledge that the act is beyond powers is not bad faith (s.40(2)(b)); no duty to enquire (s.40(2)(b)(i))
Vale Bank can enforce the loan; s.41 not relevant unless the bank is a director or connected person
Directors breached s.171 and are liable to the company; members could have restrained in advance (s.40(4)); ratification possible under s.239
Article (ii) is an outsider right; Ula cannot enforce it under s.33 even though she is a member (Eley; Hickman)
Alteration by special resolution valid under s.21 if bona fide for the benefit of the company (Allen v Gold Reefs; Citco)
No breach of contract claim unless Ula has a separate contract; possible s.994 only if membership interests are prejudiced
questions.modelAnswer:
Vale Bank. The borrowing limit restricts the directors' authority, not the company's capacity: under s.31 objects are unrestricted unless restricted and, under s.39, capacity cannot be questioned because of anything in the constitution. Under s.40, in favour of a person dealing with the company in good faith, the directors' power to bind the company is deemed free of constitutional limits. Good faith is presumed; the bank's knowledge of the article is not bad faith (s.40(2)(b)(iii)), and the bank was not required to check whether a resolution had been passed (s.40(2)(b)(i)). In any event the manager was told it had been. The loan therefore binds Thorn Ltd. Section 41 would apply only if the bank were a director or connected person.

The directors. Exceeding the limit is a breach of s.171(a) (acting in accordance with the constitution). They are liable to compensate the company for any loss, though the members may ratify under s.239, with the votes of interested directors excluded. Members could have sought to restrain the borrowing in advance under s.40(4), but cannot undo a completed transaction against the bank.

Ula. Article (ii) confers a right on Ula as accountant, not as member. Under s.33 only rights held qua member are enforceable (Eley v Positive Government Security Life Assurance; Hickman). Her 5% shareholding does not change this. The removal of the article by special resolution is valid under s.21 provided it was made bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole (Allen v Gold Reefs); replacing an accountant for business reasons plainly passes the Citco test. Ula has no claim unless she has a separate contract for services, in which case she may claim damages for its breach but cannot stop the alteration (Southern Foundries v Shirlaw [1940]). A s.994 petition is unlikely to succeed, as her interests as a member are not unfairly prejudiced.

questions.q: Wren is a director of Harbour Ltd, a boat builder. While negotiating on Harbour's behalf with a Norwegian client, Wren is told that the client will not give the contract to Harbour but would award it to Wren personally. Wren tells the board she is unwell, resigns and two months later sets up Keel Ltd, which wins the contract and makes a £400,000 profit. Meanwhile Xander, a non-executive director of Harbour, never read the financial reports sent to him and failed to notice that the finance director was taking money from the company. Advise Harbour Ltd.
markScheme: Duties owed to the company (s.170(1)); Harbour is the proper claimant
s.175: Wren exploited an opportunity learned of as director; strict liability (Regal; Bhullar)
Company's inability to obtain the contract is irrelevant (s.175(2); IDC v Cooley)
Resignation does not end the duty for opportunities learned of while a director (s.170(2)); compare Foster Bryant v Bryant on genuine resignation
No board authorisation under s.175(4)–(6); deception also suggests breach of s.172 good faith
Remedies: account of the £400,000 profit; constructive trust; Keel Ltd as knowing recipient/vehicle (s.178)
Relief under s.1157 unlikely given dishonesty
Xander: s.174 objective minimum applies to non-executives; must keep informed (Re Barings (No 5); Re D'Jan)
Causation: Harbour must show loss would have been prevented or reduced by Xander's diligence
Possible ratification (s.239) and its limits; s.232 bars exemptions
questions.modelAnswer:
Wren. The duties are owed to Harbour (s.170(1)). Under s.175(1) a director must avoid situations in which she has, or can have, an interest that conflicts with the company's, and s.175(2) applies this to exploiting property, information or opportunities, whether or not the company could take advantage of them. Wren learned of the contract while negotiating for Harbour. The facts closely match IDC v Cooley, where a managing director who feigned illness to resign and then took a contract the client would not give his company had to account for his profit. Regal (Hastings) v Gulliver confirms that good faith and the company's inability to take the opportunity are no defence.

Resignation does not help her. Under s.170(2) the s.175 duty continues after a person ceases to be a director as regards opportunities of which she became aware while a director. Cases such as Foster Bryant Surveying v Bryant [2007] show that a director who resigns for genuine reasons and is later approached may escape liability, but Wren resigned by deception in order to take the contract. There was no authorisation by independent directors under s.175(4)–(6).

Remedies (s.178) are those of equity. Harbour can claim an account of the £400,000 profit, and may argue that Keel Ltd, as Wren's vehicle, holds the contract benefit on constructive trust or is liable for knowing receipt. Relief under s.1157 requires honesty and reasonableness and is unavailable to Wren.

Xander. Under s.174 he must show the care, skill and diligence of a reasonably diligent person with the knowledge, skill and experience reasonably expected of someone in his role. Being non-executive is no excuse for ignoring board papers: directors must keep themselves informed about the company's affairs (Re Barings (No 5); Re D'Jan of London). Failing to read any financial reports falls below the objective standard. Harbour must prove causation, showing that reasonable diligence would have uncovered the theft and reduced its loss. Any exemption in the articles would be void (s.232).

questions.q: Yara, Zak and Amir each hold one-third of the shares in Comet Ltd, formed in 2018 on the understanding that all three would be directors and share profits through salaries. In 2025 Zak and Amir removed Yara as a director and began paying themselves large bonuses, so no dividends have been declared. They have also diverted a profitable contract to Nova Ltd, a company they own. They have offered to buy Yara's shares at a value fixed by Comet's auditors, discounted to reflect her minority holding. Advise Yara on her remedies.
markScheme: Foss v Harbottle: diversion is a wrong to the company; company is proper claimant
Derivative claim under s.260 for breach of ss 175/172 by Zak and Amir; two-stage permission (ss 261–263)
Ratification would be ineffective as wrongdoers' votes excluded (s.239); s.263(3) factors including availability of s.994
Reflective loss bars Yara suing personally for fall in share value caused by diversion (Marex)
s.994: Comet is a quasi-partnership (Ebrahimi); exclusion breaches the equitable understanding (O'Neill v Phillips)
Excessive remuneration and diversion of business are classic unfair prejudice
Offer: O'Neill requires a fair offer at fair value, without minority discount in a quasi-partnership, with independent valuation and costs
Discounted auditor valuation is unlikely to be a fair offer, so it does not bar the petition
s.996 remedy: buy-out at pro rata value, valuation date chosen to reflect fairness; court may account for the diverted contract in valuation
Just and equitable winding up (s.122(1)(g)) as last resort; may be refused under s.125(2)
questions.modelAnswer:
Wrongs to the company. The diversion of the contract to Nova Ltd is a breach by Zak and Amir of s.175 (and arguably s.172), and the excessive bonuses may breach s.172 or be an improper use of powers under s.171. These are wrongs to Comet Ltd, so under Foss v Harbottle the company is the proper claimant. Yara cannot sue personally for the resulting fall in her share value because of the reflective loss rule, confirmed but confined to shareholders in Sevilleja v Marex.

Derivative claim. Yara could seek permission under ss 260–264. She must first show a prima facie case (s.261). The wrongdoers cannot ratify, because under s.239 their votes are excluded, leaving only Yara. But under s.263(3)(f) the court considers whether she has a personal remedy, and the availability of s.994 may persuade it to refuse permission.

Unfair prejudice. Comet is a classic quasi-partnership under Ebrahimi v Westbourne Galleries: a small company formed on mutual trust with an understanding that all would manage and share profits through salaries. Removing Yara as director breaches that equitable understanding, and O'Neill v Phillips treats such exclusion as unfair unless she is offered a fair way out. Paying excessive bonuses instead of dividends and diverting business are also recognised forms of unfair prejudice.

The offer. Lord Hoffmann in O'Neill said an offer should be at a fair value, normally without a minority discount in a quasi-partnership, set by an independent valuer with equal access to information, and should cover costs. An auditor's valuation with a minority discount fails this test, so it does not make the petition an abuse.

Remedy. The court will probably order Zak and Amir to buy Yara's shares under s.996 at a pro rata value without discount (Re Bird Precision Bellows), adjusted to reflect the diverted contract and excessive pay, at a date that does justice. Winding up on the just and equitable ground is possible but likely refused under IA 1986 s.125(2) given the buy-out alternative.

questions.q: Finch Ltd has realised profits of £500,000 and realised losses of £320,000 on its last accounts. It also has an unrealised revaluation reserve of £150,000. The directors declare a dividend of £250,000, which is paid to its two shareholders, Gail (who is also finance director) and Hal (a passive investor who knew nothing of the accounts). Six months later Finch Ltd sells a warehouse worth £600,000 to Hal's company for £200,000. Finch Ltd is now in liquidation. Advise the liquidator.
markScheme: Distributable profits under s.830: £500,000 − £320,000 = £180,000
Revaluation reserve unrealised and excluded
Dividend of £250,000 exceeds limit by £70,000; unlawful distribution (s.830; s.836 relevant accounts)
s.847: shareholder liable if knew or had reasonable grounds to believe it unlawful; Gail clearly liable
Hal: depends on knowledge of facts; ignorance of law no defence (It's a Wrap v Gula); passive investor may escape s.847 but common law constructive trust needs knowledge
Directors who authorised it are liable for breach of duty (ss 171, 172, 174) to restore the amount (Bairstow v Queens Moat Houses)
Warehouse sale at £400,000 undervalue: disguised distribution if no genuine arm's-length intention (Aveling Barford; Progress Property)
No distributable profits remain after the dividend, so the transfer is unlawful and void/recoverable
Also consider transaction at an undervalue under IA 1986 s.238 and director liability
questions.modelAnswer:
The dividend. Under s.830 a company may distribute only profits available for the purpose: accumulated realised profits less accumulated realised losses. Finch's figure is £500,000 − £320,000 = £180,000. The £150,000 revaluation reserve is unrealised and cannot be counted. The £250,000 dividend therefore exceeds the lawful maximum by £70,000. The dividend as paid is therefore an unlawful distribution.

Recovery from shareholders. Under s.847 a member must repay a distribution if, when it was made, he knew or had reasonable grounds to believe it was unlawful. Gail, as finance director, knew the figures and is clearly liable. For Hal, It's a Wrap v Gula shows that knowledge of the facts is enough and ignorance of the law is no defence, but Hal genuinely knew nothing of the accounts, so the liquidator may struggle against him.

Recovery from directors. Directors who authorise an unlawful distribution are liable to restore it as a breach of duty: they have acted outside their powers (s.171) and, at least where they ought to have known, without due care (s.174). Bairstow v Queens Moat Houses held directors liable for the whole of an unlawful dividend, not merely the excess over what could lawfully have been paid. Gail and any other directors face this claim, subject to possible relief under s.1157 if they acted honestly and reasonably, which is unlikely for a finance director.

The warehouse. Selling a £600,000 asset to Hal's company for £200,000 transfers £400,000 of value to a shareholder's vehicle. Applying Aveling Barford v Perion and Progress Property v Moorgarth, the court asks about the real nature of the transaction. A deliberate sale at a third of market value is a disguised distribution, not a genuine arm's-length sale. Since Finch has no distributable profits left, it is unlawful and the liquidator can recover the warehouse or its value from Hal's company if it knew the facts. In addition, IA 1986 s.238 (transactions at an undervalue) may apply if Finch was insolvent at the time or became so as a result, and the directors may face misfeasance proceedings under IA 1986 s.212.

questions.q: 'The UK Corporate Governance Code's reliance on comply or explain has failed: it allows companies to ignore best practice with meaningless explanations, and real accountability requires binding legal rules.' Critically evaluate this statement.
markScheme: Explain comply or explain: Code Principles and Provisions, applied via the UK Listing Rules; 2024 Code effective 2025, Provision 29 from 2026
Rationale: flexibility, avoiding box-ticking, recognising diversity of companies (Cadbury 1992)
Market enforcement depends on shareholders reading and challenging explanations; stewardship (UK Stewardship Code)
Evidence of weaknesses: boilerplate explanations, shareholder passivity, fragmented and international ownership
Reforms: FRC emphasis on outcomes and quality reporting; 2024 Code Provision 29 internal controls declaration
Binding rules exist where needed: CA 2006 ss 168, 172, 414CZA, 439A; ECCTA 2023 and the Crime and Policing Act 2026 on corporate criminal liability
Costs of hard law: rigidity, compliance costs, one-size-fits-all; US Sarbanes-Oxley comparison
Agency theory and the role of independent directors; limits seen in corporate failures (e.g. Carillion 2018)
Balanced conclusion: hybrid model; the problem is enforcement and engagement rather than the principle itself
questions.modelAnswer:
Comply or explain dates from the Cadbury Report (1992).
