The UK Corporate Governance Code, now the 2024 version applying to financial years from 1 January 2025, sets out Principles that companies must apply and Provisions they must follow or explain departures from. The UK Listing Rules require this disclosure from in-scope companies. The theory is that flexibility allows each company to adopt arrangements suited to its circumstances, while shareholders, as owners, judge whether explanations are adequate and act through voting and engagement.

The statement has some force. Many explanations are boilerplate, and the model relies on engaged shareholders. Ownership of UK listed companies is now fragmented and largely overseas, and index funds may lack incentives to scrutinise individual explanations. High-profile failures such as Carillion (2018) showed boards apparently compliant with the Code yet failing on risk and controls. The FRC has repeatedly criticised the quality of reporting.

However, the claim that the model has failed overstates the case. Compliance with most Provisions is high, and departures are often well reasoned, for example a temporary combined chair and chief executive during a crisis. The UK already uses hard law where binding rules are justified: removal of directors (s.168), the s.172 duty and s.172 statement (s.414CZA), binding votes on pay policy (s.439A) and corporate criminal liability reforms in the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, extended to all offences by the Crime and Policing Act 2026. The 2024 Code also responds to concerns by requiring a board declaration on the effectiveness of material internal controls (Provision 29) instead of a US-style legal certification regime.

Binding rules have costs. The US Sarbanes-Oxley Act 2002 imposed heavy compliance costs and may have encouraged box-ticking. A uniform rule cannot account for differences between a FTSE 100 bank and a small listed company.

The better view is that comply or explain is sound in principle, but works only if explanations are meaningful and investors engage. The answer lies in stronger stewardship, better FRC monitoring and targeted hard law where self-regulation repeatedly fails, rather than wholesale replacement.

questions.q: On 1 March, Ivy agreed to buy from Jet Ltd (i) a specific vintage printing press, which Jet agreed to repaint before delivery, and (ii) 200 tonnes of paper out of 1,000 tonnes stored in Jet's warehouse, paid for in advance. On 5 March Jet finished repainting the press but did not tell Ivy. On 6 March a fire destroyed the warehouse, the press and 300 tonnes of paper. Jet Ltd has gone into liquidation. Ivy is a business buyer. Advise Ivy.
markScheme: Business sale: SGA 1979 governs; CRA s.29 not applicable
Property passes when intended (s.17); otherwise s.18 rules
Press is specific goods not in a deliverable state; Rule 2 applies
Under Rule 2 property passes only when the work is done and the buyer has notice; no notice by 6 March
Property and risk remained with Jet (s.20(1)); Ivy need not pay and may recover any price paid as a creditor
Paper: unascertained goods from a bulk; s.16 means no property until ascertainment
But ss 20A–20B: Ivy paid for a specified quantity from an identified bulk, so she is an owner in common
s.20A(3): share = quantity paid for and due ÷ quantity in bulk at that time: 200/1,000 before the fire, 200/700 after
s.20A(4) reduces shares only if buyers' shares together exceed the bulk; assuming no other paying buyers, the loss falls on Jet's own portion and Ivy can claim all 200 tonnes from the liquidator
questions.modelAnswer:
Ivy is a business buyer, so the SGA 1979 applies and CRA 2015 s.29 does not. Property passes when the parties intend (s.17); absent contrary intention, the s.18 rules apply, and risk passes with property (s.20(1)).

The press. The press was specific goods, but Jet had to repaint it before delivery, so it was not in a deliverable state. Under s.18 Rule 2, property passes only when the seller does the work and the buyer has notice that it has been done. Jet finished on 5 March but did not tell Ivy, so property had not passed by 6 March. Risk therefore remained with Jet. The press is destroyed at Jet's risk and Ivy is not liable for the price. Any part of the price she paid is recoverable only as an unsecured creditor.

The paper. The 200 tonnes were unascertained goods forming part of an identified bulk. Under s.16 no property passes in unascertained goods until ascertained, which would leave Ivy unsecured (Re Goldcorp). However, ss 20A–20B now apply because Ivy contracted for a specified quantity from an identified bulk and paid in advance. She therefore became an owner in common of the bulk. Under s.20A(3) her undivided share at any time is the quantity paid for and due to her divided by the quantity then in the bulk: 200 ÷ 1,000 before the fire.

The fire destroyed 300 tonnes, leaving 700. Her share is recalculated as 200 ÷ 700, about 28.6%. Section 20A(4) reduces buyers' shares proportionately only where the buyers' shares together would exceed the whole bulk. Assuming no other buyers had paid for paper from this bulk, the remaining 700 tonnes easily cover her 200, so the loss falls on Jet's own unsold portion. Because her interest is proprietary, Ivy can claim all 200 tonnes from the liquidator ahead of unsecured creditors. If other prepaid buyers' claims exceeded 700 tonnes, each share would be scaled down and she would be an unsecured creditor for any shortfall.

questions.q: 'The nemo dat rule and its exceptions represent an incoherent compromise between protecting ownership and promoting commercial certainty.' Discuss, with reference to the Sale of Goods Act 1979 and relevant case law.
markScheme: Explain nemo dat (s.21) and the policy tension between security of property and security of transactions (Bishopsgate Motor Finance v Transport Brakes [1949], Denning LJ)
Estoppel exception: narrow, requires representation by owner (Moorgate Mercantile v Twitchings [1977])
Mercantile agents (Factors Act 1889 s.2): requires possession with owner's consent in capacity as agent, ordinary course of business
Voidable title (s.23) and the timing of avoidance (Car & Universal Finance v Caldwell)
Seller in possession (s.24) and buyer in possession (s.25); Newtons of Wembley v Williams [1965]; National Employers' Mutual v Jones [1990]
Shogun Finance v Hudson [2003]: face-to-face versus written dealings; criticised distinction
Hire Purchase Act 1964 Pt III: protection limited to private purchasers of motor vehicles
Incoherence arguments: arbitrary lines, outcomes depending on chance (whether contract void or voidable, how rogue dealt)
Defence of the rules: allocates loss to party best placed to avoid it; reform proposals (Law Commission work) not enacted
Alternatives: good-faith purchaser rule; apportionment of loss; registration systems
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The starting point is s.21 SGA 1979: a buyer from a non-owner without authority gets no better title than the seller had. Denning LJ in Bishopsgate Motor Finance v Transport Brakes [1949] identified the competing principles of protecting property and protecting commercial transactions. The exceptions try to balance them, but critics say they do so arbitrarily.

The exceptions vary widely. Estoppel needs a representation or negligence by the owner and is read narrowly (Moorgate Mercantile v Twitchings [1977]). The Factors Act 1889 s.2 protects buyers from mercantile agents acting in the ordinary course of business. Section 23 protects good-faith buyers from a seller with an unavoided voidable title, yet Car & Universal Finance v Caldwell allowed avoidance simply by telling the police. Newtons of Wembley v Williams [1965] then let a rogue pass title under s.25 even after avoidance, undermining Caldwell, while National Employers' Mutual v Jones [1990] held that s.25 cannot cure an original theft.

The strongest case for incoherence is mistaken identity. In Shogun Finance v Hudson [2003] the majority held a written agreement with a rogue impersonating a named person void, so s.23 failed, whereas face-to-face dealings are presumed to create a voidable contract (Phillips v Brooks [1919]). The innocent buyer's protection thus depends on how the rogue happened to deal. Part III of the Hire Purchase Act 1964 protects only private buyers of motor vehicles.

The rules can be defended. They tend to put loss on the party who took the risk, such as an owner who entrusts goods to an agent, and they keep ownership as the default, which supports secured lending and retention of title. Apportioning loss between innocent parties, suggested by Devlin LJ in Ingram v Little [1961], was rejected by the Law Reform Committee.

The law is therefore a set of market-specific exceptions rather than a principle, and outcomes can turn on chance. A single good-faith purchaser rule with an exception for stolen goods, as in many civil law systems, would be more coherent.

questions.q: Kai is the purchasing manager of Loom Ltd, with authority to sign supply contracts up to £50,000. Loom's managing director tells Mill Ltd, a regular supplier, 'Kai handles all our cotton orders'. Kai orders £120,000 of cotton from Mill Ltd. He also signs a £30,000 contract with Nest Ltd in his own name without mentioning Loom, intending it to be for Loom. Separately, Kai receives a secret £5,000 commission from Mill Ltd. Advise Loom Ltd.
markScheme: Actual authority limited to £50,000; Mill contract exceeds it
Apparent authority: MD's representation to Mill; MD has actual authority to make it (Freeman & Lockyer)
Reliance and change of position by Mill; Mill not on notice of the limit
Loom likely bound to Mill; Loom can sue Kai for exceeding authority
Nest contract within actual authority; undisclosed principal doctrine: Loom can sue and be sued unless excluded or identity important (Siu Yin Kwan)
Kai also personally liable on the Nest contract; Nest may elect
Secret commission: breach of fiduciary duty; held on constructive trust for Loom (FHR European Ventures v Cedar)
Loom may rescind the Mill contract as tainted by the bribe and claim against Mill; dismissal of Kai
questions.modelAnswer:
The Mill contract. Kai's actual authority is limited to £50,000, so the £120,000 order is outside it. The question is apparent authority. Under Freeman & Lockyer v Buckhurst Park, Loom is bound if it represented to Mill that Kai had authority, Mill relied on that and altered its position. The managing director, who has actual authority to manage the business, told Mill that Kai 'handles all our cotton orders'. That is a representation by the principal, not a self-authorisation by Kai of the kind rejected in The Ocean Frost. Mill relied on it by accepting and fulfilling the order. Unless Mill knew of the £50,000 limit, or the size of the order should have put it on inquiry, Loom is bound. Loom can claim against Kai for any loss caused by his breach of his duty to obey instructions.

The Nest contract. The £30,000 contract was within Kai's actual authority, but he contracted in his own name, so Loom is an undisclosed principal. Under Siu Yin Kwan v Eastern Insurance, an undisclosed principal can sue and be sued on a contract made within actual authority unless the terms exclude this or the third party had good reason to deal only with the agent. Nothing suggests either, so Loom can enforce the contract. Nest can sue either Kai or Loom once it discovers Loom, subject to the rules on election.

The secret commission. An agent must not make a secret profit or allow his interest to conflict with his principal's. The £5,000 is a bribe. Following FHR European Ventures v Cedar Capital Partners, it is held on constructive trust for Loom, giving Loom a proprietary claim to it and anything it was used to buy. Loom can also dismiss Kai and recover losses. Against Mill, the payment of a bribe to Loom's agent allows Loom to rescind the cotton contract, if restitution is possible, or recover the amount of the bribe or its losses from Mill.

questions.q: Ola, a self-employed agent, has for six years negotiated the sale of Pine Ltd's garden furniture to retailers in Scotland on commission. Pine Ltd terminates the agreement with one month's notice. Separately, before Rush Ltd was incorporated, its promoter Tom signed a lease 'for and on behalf of Rush Ltd'. After incorporation, the board resolved to 'ratify' the lease, but the landlord now sues Tom for unpaid rent. Advise Ola and Tom.
markScheme: Ola is a commercial agent: self-employed, continuing authority to negotiate sale of goods for another (reg 2, 1993 Regulations)
Minimum notice: three months after three or more years (reg 15); one month is insufficient
Damages for short notice; plus compensation under reg 17 (default) unless contract provides for indemnity
Compensation based on value of the agency at termination: what a hypothetical purchaser would pay (Lonsdale v Howard & Hallam)
Claim must be notified within one year of termination (reg 17(9)); exceptions under reg 18
Tom: pre-incorporation contract; s.51 CA 2006 makes Tom personally liable subject to contrary agreement
'For and on behalf of' wording is not a contrary agreement (Phonogram v Lane [1982])
Company cannot ratify: it did not exist when the contract was made (Kelner v Baxter)
Novation needed: a new contract between Rush and the landlord releases Tom; board resolution alone insufficient
Tom may have an indemnity claim if Rush agreed, and possibly an argument that a new lease was formed by conduct
questions.modelAnswer:
Ola. Under reg 2 of the Commercial Agents (Council Directive) Regulations 1993, a commercial agent is a self-employed intermediary with continuing authority to negotiate the sale or purchase of goods on behalf of a principal. Ola fits this definition. Regulation 15 sets minimum notice periods: one month in the first year, two in the second and three in the third and later years. After six years Ola was entitled to at least three months' notice, so one month is insufficient, and she can claim damages for the shortfall.

She is also entitled on termination to compensation under reg 17, unless her contract provides for an indemnity instead. Compensation is the default. In Lonsdale v Howard & Hallam the House of Lords held it should reflect the value of the agency on the date of termination, broadly what a hypothetical purchaser would pay for the right to receive future commission, which in a declining market may be modest. Ola must notify Pine of her intention to claim within one year of termination (reg 17(9)). No reg 18 exclusion seems to apply.

Tom. The lease was made before Rush Ltd existed. Under CA 2006 s.51(1), a contract that purports to be made by or on behalf of an unformed company takes effect, subject to any contrary agreement, as one made with the person acting for it, who is personally liable. Signing 'for and on behalf of' the company is not a contrary agreement; in Phonogram v Lane the Court of Appeal held that clear exclusion of personal liability is required.

The board's purported ratification is ineffective. Ratification needs a principal in existence when the act was done (Kelner v Baxter), so a company cannot ratify a pre-incorporation contract. Only a novation, a new contract between Rush and the landlord, would release Tom. Tom remains liable, though he may seek an indemnity from Rush if it agreed to assume the lease.

questions.q: 'The codification of directors' duties in the Companies Act 2006, and in particular the adoption of enlightened shareholder value in s.172, changed very little in practice.' Critically discuss.
markScheme: Background: Company Law Review; aims of codification (accessibility, clarity) and s.170(3)–(4) continuity with common law
Enlightened shareholder value v pluralism debate; CLR rejected pluralism
s.172 structure: subjective good faith test (Regentcrest); factors are matters to have regard to, not independent duties
Enforcement gap: owed to company; stakeholders cannot sue; derivative claim limits (s.263); few successful s.172 claims
Sequana (2022): s.172(3) and creditors; development of law through s.172 rather than common law alone
Changes elsewhere: s.175 authorisation by independent directors; s.170(2) post-resignation; derivative claim reform; s.174 objective standard
Reporting: s.414CZA s.172 statement (2018 Regulations) and effect on board processes
Evidence of practice: board minutes, process-driven compliance, risk of box-ticking
Comparisons: proposals for purpose-based reform (e.g. Better Business Act campaign); ESG and climate litigation (ClientEarth v Shell [2023])
Reasoned conclusion on degree of change
questions.modelAnswer:
Following the Company Law Review (CLR), the Companies Act 2006 codified directors' duties to make the law accessible and to state the company's purpose. But s.170(3)–(4) requires the duties to be read in line with the earlier case law, which points to continuity.

The CLR rejected pluralism in favour of enlightened shareholder value: under s.172 directors promote the company's success for the benefit of its members, having regard to factors such as employees, the environment and long-term consequences. The core test remains the subjective good faith test of Re Smith & Fawcett [1942], applied in Regentcrest v Cohen. The factors are matters to consider, not separate duties, and courts rarely second-guess commercial judgment. On this view s.172 restated the old law.

Enforcement supports this. Duties are owed to the company (s.170(1)), so stakeholders cannot sue, and shareholders face the s.263 permission hurdle. In ClientEarth v Shell [2023] permission to continue a climate-related derivative claim was refused, showing how hard it is to use s.172 to force stakeholder-oriented decisions.

Yet change has occurred. Sequana [2022] used s.172(3) to clarify when creditors' interests must be considered. The s.172 statement (s.414CZA, from 2019) makes large companies explain how directors had regard to the factors, changing board processes. Elsewhere, codification changed substance: s.175 lets independent directors authorise conflicts, s.170(2) extends the conflict duty after resignation, s.174 confirmed the objective standard and Part 11 created the statutory derivative claim.

Critics say the statement encourages box-ticking and that real change requires reform of corporate purpose, as the Better Business Act campaign proposes.

Conclusion. As to enforceable outcomes, the proposition is largely right: s.172 has not changed whose interests directors ultimately serve or created new claimants. But codification altered conflicts, derivative claims and reporting, and s.172 now frames the law's development, as Sequana shows. The change lies more in process and disclosure than in substance.

questions.q: 'The capital maintenance doctrine is an outdated and ineffective means of protecting creditors, and should be replaced by a solvency-based test for all distributions.' Discuss.
markScheme: Purpose of capital maintenance: creditor protection as quid pro quo for limited liability (Trevor v Whitworth)
Elements: no discount (s.580), distribution rules (ss 829–831), buy-back and reduction rules, financial assistance (public companies)
Weaknesses: no minimum capital for private companies; nominal capital meaningless; legal capital not linked to risk
Distribution rules depend on accounts and accounting standards; realised profits concept (s.853, ICAEW TECH guidance)
Creditors protected better by contract (adjusting creditors), insolvency law (ss 213, 214, 238, 423 IA 1986), directors' duties (Sequana)
Existing solvency-based mechanisms: private company reduction (s.641) and buy-back from capital (s.709) using solvency statements
Arguments for solvency tests: flexibility, focus on ability to pay debts; comparisons (US Model Business Corporation Act, New Zealand)
Arguments against: reliance on directors' judgment, enforcement problems, EU legacy for public companies
Recent case law shows enduring relevance (Aveling Barford; Progress Property; Sequana)
Reform proposals, e.g. the 2021 white paper Restoring trust in audit and corporate governance on disclosure of distributable reserves, and conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Capital maintenance, developed in cases such as Trevor v Whitworth (1887), is the price of limited liability: since creditors cannot pursue members, capital should not be returned to them. It now comprises rules against issuing shares at a discount (s.580), the restrictions on distributions (ss 829–831), procedures for reductions of capital and share buy-backs, and the prohibition on financial assistance for public companies.

There are strong arguments that the doctrine is outdated. Private companies need no minimum capital, so a company can be formed with £1, and the £50,000 minimum for public companies is trivial for large businesses. The distribution rules depend on accounting concepts, notably 'realised profits' (s.853), which are complex and shaped by accounting standards rather than creditor needs.

Creditors arguably have better protection elsewhere. Insolvency law offers wrongful and fraudulent trading (IA 1986 ss 213–214), transactions at an undervalue (s.238) and transactions defrauding creditors (s.423). Directors must consider creditors' interests as insolvency approaches (BTI v Sequana [2022]).

The UK already uses solvency tests in some contexts. Private companies can reduce capital by special resolution and a directors' solvency statement (s.641), and buy back shares out of capital with a solvency statement (s.709). New Zealand and US states following the Model Business Corporation Act use solvency-based distribution tests.

However, a solvency-only approach has risks. It relies on directors' judgment, which may be optimistic, and on liquidators suing after failure. The current rules provide a clear, accountant-checked boundary. Aveling Barford and Progress Property show the rules catching disguised returns of value, while Sequana, where a dividend lawful under Part 23 was challenged under directors' duties, shows the regimes complementing each other.

Conclusion. The doctrine is imperfect, and minimum capital in particular has little value. But the case for abolishing the balance-sheet test is weaker. A combined model, keeping the realised-profits test as a floor while adding a mandatory solvency statement for distributions, as some reform proposals have suggested, would target the real risk, which is the company's ability to pay its debts as they fall due, without losing the certainty of the current regime.
